description: We are a team of engineers from Ecuador building an interactive browser game for students. We love space exploration, 3D web and turning real NASA data into experiences that kids can play and learn from. Our team is complete, but we are happy to connect with other teams, mentors and space enthusiasts at the Sangolquí event :D
summary: Shackleton: Night Shift is a free web game for kids aged 7 to 12, in English and Spanish, built for the “Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer” challenge. Players run the first human base at the Moon’s south pole for 30 days by touching a living 3D model: every day they split limited solar and battery energy between air and water, food, radiation shielding and the workshop. They must survive six days of lunar night and solar storms that are real events from NASA’s DONKI space-weather database, choosing between sheltering the crew or keeping the base running. Ten short mini-games turn real mission skills into play, like driving a rover to the ice, building a regolith wall or docking the relief ship. Every choice has a cost, failure is a gentle “mission aborted”, and the ending explains what a real mission would do. It runs in any browser, on phones and offline, with no account. It matters because children feel the real trade-offs of living on the Moon, and every number in the game says honestly whether it is real data, simulated or a design choice.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Shackleton: Night Shift puts a child (ages 7–12) in charge of a small lunar base in 2048, at Shackleton crater on the Moon's south pole, for 30 days. There is no character walking around: the player manages the whole base by tapping a living 3D model or using a control panel. Each day the player shares out the energy from the Sun and the battery among four modules (air and water, food, radiation shielding, workshop), immediately sees how each resource will change, and then plays the day.

The game is split into 5 acts that unlock one real mission trade-off at a time:

- Limited energy: there is never enough for everything.

- Lunar night: six days with no Sun; you only have what you saved.

- Solar storms: shelter the crew (little radiation, no production) or keep working (more radiation).

- Breakdowns and lunar dust: fixing today costs energy, waiting costs production.

- Communications: with the antenna powered, the storm warning arrives two days earlier.

Every event offers two valid options with different costs. Ten mini-games spread across the month turn mission skills into play: driving a rover to the ice, tuning space-weather antennas, finding air leaks, routing cables, steering a robotic arm, checking the crew's health, building a regolith radiation wall, aiming a micrometeorite shield, preparing for a great solar storm and docking the relief ship. Each starts with an animated demo, so children who read little can still play. There are three modes (guided Tutorial, Cadet, Commander) and an ending that explains what happened and how a real mission would handle it.

HOW IT USES NASA DATA

The solar storms are real coronal mass ejections and solar energetic particle events from NASA DONKI. A script downloads a year of events, normalizes them and assigns each a strength level from 1 to 4; the game engine picks a real storm of the right level for each act without altering its data. If the Sun is active today, a small serverless proxy fetches the live DONKI event, so the first storm is this week's real one (the NASA API key never reaches the browser, and the game falls back to stored data if the API is down). Real doses measured on the International Space Station (RadLab / OSDR) let players compare their crew's radiation with reality; NASA OSDR studies feed a "Real science" card at the end; Blue Marble is the Earth in the lunar sky; and Canadian Space Agency material provides the food-production facts. An in-game panel, "Where does the data come from?", lists every source with a link and an honest status: real data, simulated, or game design decision.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Children experience, not just read about, the real trade-offs of a lunar mission: power budgets, the long polar night, space weather and radiation protection. Mistakes are framed as learning ("mission aborted", never death), each challenge leaves one short science idea, and the ending connects play to real missions. Because it is free, bilingual (English/Spanish), runs on low-cost phones and works offline once loaded, it can be used in classrooms with poor connectivity.

Next steps: run more play-tests with children and teachers, write a short teacher guide, and add real south-pole terrain from NASA's CGI Moon Kit.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

TypeScript, Astro, Preact with signals, Three.js (3D), a Vercel serverless function for the space-weather proxy, Supabase as a data backup, Blender (Python scripts to model the base). The game engine is pure and deterministic: the same seed and the same decisions always give the same result, and a 1000-game automated simulation is used to tune difficulty. All balance numbers live in JSON files, not in code. Open source under the MIT license.

CREATIVITY AND FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Instead of a quiz, the whole base is a toy you touch. Most importantly, we had children play-test the game during development and changed it based on what they told us and what we saw them struggle with:

- They got lost in the mini-games, so we added an animated tutorial before each one; the clock doesn't start until they are ready.

- Some words were too technical, so we rewrote every text in short, simple sentences in English and Spanish.

- The interface felt complicated, so we made it simpler and more visual: drawings and icons instead of labels, energy shown as blocks, and fewer things on screen at once.

- They connected more with the crew when it felt alive, so we added astronaut faces that show emotions (happy, calm, worried, scared) as the base changes.

We also designed for accessibility: state is never shown by color alone, everything works with the keyboard, a 2D panel works without 3D, "reduce motion" is respected and graphics adapt to slow devices. We reviewed tone with child-development criteria (no death, no scary failure: the mission is "aborted" and the game explains why), used no NASA logos, and kept a strict line between real science and game fiction so children and teachers always know which is which.
